section.title: The Sealed and the Great Multitude
section.sectionRationale: Chapter 6 ended with terrified sinners asking who can withstand the day of the Lamb's wrath. Chapter 7 answers directly, as a deliberate interlude between the sixth and seventh seals: the four winds of judgment are held back while God's servants are sealed, first a numbered 144,000 from Israel's tribes, then an uncountable multitude from every nation, robed in white and secure before the throne. This is one self-contained scene of comfort before the seventh seal resumes the judgment sequence in chapter 8.
section.thesis: Before the winds of judgment are released, God seals His own so that none of them is lost, and John's vision widens from a precisely numbered 144,000 from Israel's tribes to an uncountable multitude from every nation, both secure before the throne, robed in white, and forever sheltered by the Lamb who is their shepherd.
section.frameNote: Four beats: four angels holding back the winds while the servants of God are sealed; the sealing of the 144,000 from the twelve tribes; the great multitude from every nation crying salvation before the throne; and the elder's explanation of who they are and what awaits them.

verses.text: After this I saw four angels standing at the four corners of the earth, holding back its four winds so that no wind would blow on land or sea or on any tree.
And I saw another angel ascending from the east, with the seal of the living God. And he called out in a loud voice to the four angels who had been given power to harm the land and the sea:
“Do not harm the land or sea or trees until we have {{sphragizo|sealed}} the foreheads of the servants of our God.”
And I heard the number of those who were sealed, 144,000 from all the tribes of Israel:
From the tribe of Judah 12,000 were sealed, from the tribe of Reuben 12,000, from the tribe of Gad 12,000,
from the tribe of Asher 12,000, from the tribe of Naphtali 12,000, from the tribe of Manasseh 12,000,
from the tribe of Simeon 12,000, from the tribe of Levi 12,000, from the tribe of Issachar 12,000,
from the tribe of Zebulun 12,000, from the tribe of Joseph 12,000, and from the tribe of Benjamin 12,000.

After this I looked and saw a multitude too large to count, from every nation and tribe and people and tongue, standing before the throne and before the Lamb. They were wearing white robes and holding palm branches in their hands.
And they cried out in a loud voice: “Salvation to our God, who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb!”
And all the angels stood around the throne and around the elders and the four living creatures. And they fell facedown before the throne and worshiped God,
saying, “Amen! Blessing and glory and wisdom and thanks and honor and power and strength be to our God forever and ever! Amen.”

units.label: Who they are
units.note: washed in the blood of the Lamb

verses.text: Then one of the elders addressed me: “These in white robes,” he asked, “who are they, and where have they come from?”
“Sir,” I answered, “you know.” So he replied, “These are the ones who have come out of the {{thlipsis|great tribulation}}; they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.
For this reason, they are before the throne of God and serve Him day and night in His temple; and the One seated on the throne will spread His {{skenoo|tabernacle}} over them.
‘Never again will they hunger, and never will they thirst; nor will the sun beat down upon them, nor any scorching heat.’
For the Lamb in the center of the throne will be their {{poimaino|shepherd}}. ‘He will lead them to springs of living water,’ and ‘God will wipe away every tear from their eyes.’ ”

sphragizo.gloss: To seal, to mark with a seal of ownership and protection. The seal placed on the forehead of God's servants echoes the blood on Israel's doorposts at the Passover and Ezekiel's mark on the foreheads of the faithful in Jerusalem, a sign that these belong to God and are kept safe under His authority through coming judgment.

thlipsis.gloss: Pressure, affliction, tribulation. The definite article marks this as 'the' great tribulation, the specific, intense suffering these worshipers have passed through. The word describes real, crushing hardship, yet these very people now stand triumphant before the throne, their robes made white, not despite the tribulation but through the Lamb's blood applied to it.

skenoo.gloss: To tabernacle, to pitch one's tent, to dwell. The same word John uses in his Gospel to say the Word became flesh and 'tabernacled' among us. Here God promises to spread His tabernacling presence over the redeemed permanently, the goal toward which the whole story of God dwelling with His people, from the wilderness tent to Christ's incarnation, has been moving.

poimaino.gloss: To shepherd, to tend and guide a flock. It is a striking paradox that the Lamb Himself will be the flock's shepherd, echoing Psalm 23 and Ezekiel 34's promise of God as shepherd, now fulfilled by the Lamb who leads His people to springs of living water and wipes every tear from their eyes.

basic.context: Before judgment resumes, John sees four angels holding back destructive winds so that another angel can first seal the foreheads of God's servants, a precisely numbered 144,000 drawn from Israel's twelve tribes. Then the vision widens dramatically: an uncountable multitude from every nation, tribe, people, and language stands before the throne in white robes, crying out that salvation belongs to God and the Lamb. An elder explains that these have come out of great tribulation, washed white by the Lamb's blood, and are promised that the Lamb Himself, their shepherd, will lead them to living water and wipe away every tear.
basic.hermeneutics: This chapter answers chapter 6's terrified question, who can withstand the day of wrath, by showing that God's own people are sealed and secure. People debate whether the 144,000 and the great multitude are the same group seen from two angles or two distinct groups, and whether the 144,000 refers to ethnic Israel or symbolically to the whole church; the chapter itself does not force one answer, but its comfort does not depend on resolving every detail: God's people, however numbered, are never lost.
basic.originalLanguages: God's servants are sphragizo, sealed, marked as His own and kept safe, recalling the blood on Israel's doorposts at Passover. These are called out of the thlipsis, the great tribulation, real and crushing affliction, yet made triumphant. God promises to skenoo, tabernacle, dwell permanently among them, the same word John uses of the Word becoming flesh. And astonishingly, the Lamb will poimaino, shepherd, His flock, leading them to living water and wiping away every tear.
basic.typology: The sealing of foreheads fulfills Ezekiel's vision of a mark placed on the faithful before judgment struck Jerusalem, and echoes the Passover blood that spared Israel's firstborn. The palm branches recall both the Feast of Tabernacles and Christ's triumphal entry. And the promise that the Lamb will shepherd His people and wipe away every tear fulfills Psalm 23, Ezekiel 34, and Isaiah's promise that God would swallow up death and wipe tears from every face.
basic.christ: The Lamb stands at the center of the throne, receiving worship equal to God's alongside the redeemed multitude's cry of salvation, and it is His blood, not merely their own endurance, that washes their robes white. In the chapter's most striking paradox, this Lamb becomes the flock's shepherd, fulfilling the ancient promise that God Himself would shepherd His people, now accomplished through the very one who was slain for them.
basic.god: God is the one who seals His servants before judgment falls, ensuring not one of His own is swept away with the wicked. He is also the one who will tabernacle among the redeemed forever, and who personally wipes every tear from their eyes, showing that His justice toward the world and His tenderness toward His people are two expressions of the same unwavering faithfulness.
basic.crossReferences: Ezekiel 9:4-6 pictures a mark placed on the foreheads of the faithful before judgment strikes Jerusalem, the pattern behind this chapter's sealing. Isaiah 49:10 and Psalm 23:1 supply the images of shepherding and provision fulfilled in verses 16-17. Isaiah 25:8 promises that God will wipe away tears from every face, quoted almost directly in verse 17.
basic.oneStory: From the Passover lamb's blood on Israel's doorposts to Ezekiel's mark on the faithful in a doomed city, the Bible has long promised that God distinguishes and protects His own people even as judgment falls on a rebellious world. Here that promise reaches its fullest expression: a sealed and countless people from every nation, washed in the blood of the Lamb, forever sheltered by the very Lamb who will shepherd them to living water and wipe every tear from their eyes.

context.literary:
The chapter opens with 'After this' and then repeats it at verse 9, and the two phrases mark the two halves of the scene: the sealing of those who are counted, verses 1 to 8, and the gathering of those who cannot be counted, verses 9 to 17. John writes, 'I heard the number', verse 4, and then 'I looked and saw a multitude too large to count', verse 9. The contrast between what he hears and what he sees is the key to the chapter. Hearing gives the arithmetic, seeing gives the crowd.

A pattern John uses elsewhere in the book is at work here. In chapter 5 he heard of a Lion of Judah and turned to see a Lamb. In chapter 7 he hears of the tribes of Israel and turns to see every nation. In both cases the first image is the Old Testament promise and the second is its fulfilment, and the second does not cancel the first but opens it out.

The list of the tribes is carefully built. Judah comes first, in place of Reuben the firstborn, and each tribe receives the same twelve thousand, so that no tribe is more favoured than another. The sealing is therefore a picture of completeness and equality, not a census. The list also differs from the usual order, includes Levi, which received no territory, and leaves out Dan and Ephraim, putting Joseph and Manasseh in their place.

The second half has the form of a worship scene with a question and answer. The multitude sings, the angels respond with a sevenfold doxology of their own, verse 12, and then an elder asks the question that John cannot answer, so that the explanation comes from heaven rather than from the seer's own insight. The chapter closes with Old Testament promises that are now said in the present, so the last four verses are a catalogue of things that will never again be a danger: hunger, thirst, scorching sun, tears.
context.historical:
The picture of angels holding back winds comes from the world of the Old Testament, where wind is a messenger and a weapon, and the 'four corners of the earth' is a way of speaking of the whole world as the ancient mind pictured it, with north, south, east and west. The angel who has the seal ascends 'from the east', the direction from which the sun rises, which is also the direction of the garden and of the glory of the LORD in Ezekiel 43:2.

A seal in the ancient world was a signet that marked ownership and guaranteed security. Merchants sealed goods, kings sealed decrees, and owners marked their slaves and their cattle. The believers in Asia Minor lived among those who carried the mark of the beast, Revelation 13:16 and 17, and the seal on the forehead is the reverse of that: it says whose they are, and it says it in the most visible place.

The twelve tribes did not exist in this form for John's hearers. The northern tribes had been carried off by Assyria some eight centuries earlier, and Judah and Benjamin had been exiled to Babylon. Yet the Jewish and Christian imagination still held the picture of the whole people restored, as in Ezekiel 37 and 48. A hearer who saw twelve tribes listed would hear a promise of regathering and of a people complete in the eyes of God.

The white robes and the palm branches belong to the festivals of Israel. Palms were gathered at the Feast of Tabernacles, Leviticus 23:40, a festival of thanksgiving at the harvest and a memory of the wilderness shelters, and the crowd at Jesus' entry into Jerusalem waved palm branches too, John 12:13. John's readers were suffering, and some were being killed for the name of Jesus. The scene tells them where those who die end up: not in the dust, but on their feet before God, holding branches of victory.
context.canonical:
The sealing is rooted in Ezekiel 9:4, where a man is told to put a mark on the foreheads of those who sigh and groan over the abominations in Jerusalem, so that they would be spared when the executioners passed through. The Passover is behind it too, since the blood on the doorposts marked the houses the destroyer would pass over, Exodus 12:13. Elsewhere in the New Testament the seal is the Holy Spirit, who marks believers as God's own until the day of redemption, Ephesians 1:13 and Ephesians 4:30, and Paul tells the Corinthians that God has set His seal on us, 2 Corinthians 1:22.

The 144,000 return in chapter 14, where they stand with the Lamb on Mount Zion with His name and His Father's name on their foreheads, Revelation 14:1, and the same name on the forehead is the reward of all God's servants in the new Jerusalem, Revelation 22:4. The list of tribes is echoed in the twelve gates of the city, Revelation 21:12, so the people counted here are the people whose names are carved into the final home.

The great multitude is the fulfilment of the promise to Abraham that all the families of the earth would be blessed through him, Genesis 12:3, and of Genesis 15:5, where his seed would be as numerous as the stars. It is also the new song of Revelation 5:9, where people from every tribe and tongue and people and nation are purchased by blood. The closing promises are taken from Isaiah 49:10 and Isaiah 25:8, from the shepherd of Psalm 23 and Ezekiel 34, and are picked up in Revelation 21:4. The 'tabernacle' of verse 15 is the dwelling of John 1:14 and the dwelling of Revelation 21:3, a thread that runs from Sinai to the new creation.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
John wants the suffering churches to hear two things in the right order. First, that the winds do not blow until God's people are sealed, which means that judgment is not allowed to catch them unawares or take one of them by mistake. The sealing comes before the harm, and the harm waits for the sealing. Second, that the sealed are not a thin remnant but a throng. The hearers who may feel few and weak are shown a crowd that no one can number, from the whole earth.

He also means the reader to see the way the picture is built: what John hears is the Israel of the promises, and what he sees is the world gathered into that promise. The point is not to cut the nations out of Israel's story but to show that the story was always meant for them. A Gentile believer in Ephesus or Laodicea who had been wondering whether he belonged to the people of the Messiah is told in the plainest way that he does.

Lastly, John means the elder's words to shape how the church thinks of its present trouble. The multitude has come 'out of the great tribulation', and the way out is by washing, not by escaping. The words are a pastoral instruction that tribulation is expected, that the robe is washed in blood and not by effort, and that the end of it is the shepherding of the Lamb and the wiping away of every tear. A church that knows its end can bear its middle.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes what John saw and what an elder said. It gives no instruction to count, to claim a tribe, or to look for a mark on the forehead. Readers who have tried to identify the 144,000 with a particular movement, or to make a sealing into a rite that a person must receive, have gone beyond what the text says. The seal in the New Testament is the Spirit given to every believer, and not a ritual to be sought.

What the chapter does prescribe, by implication, is the posture of the multitude, which is also the posture of the church. They cry out salvation to God and to the Lamb, they fall on their faces in worship, and they serve day and night. That response is the one to bring now. The description of what will never happen again, no hunger, no thirst, no tears, is a promise and a comfort. It is not a rebuke to those who weep now, since the Lamb himself will do the wiping. Believers can apply the passage by taking courage in tribulation, by refusing to separate Israel's promises from the church's inheritance, and by worshipping with the same song now, as the church on earth is invited to do.

debates.question: Who are the 144,000?

views.label: Ethnic Israel, believing Jews
views.case: The text says 'from all the tribes of Israel', names each tribe, and gives each the same number, which is how one would describe a literal people. Paul expects a future salvation of Israel, Romans 11:26, and some readers take the sealing as a sign that God has not finished with His covenant people. The list is placed apart from the multitude of the nations, and John says he 'heard' the number and 'saw' the multitude as though they were different groups.

views.label: The whole church, in Israel's dress
views.case: Revelation speaks of the church in Old Testament terms, as a kingdom and priests, Revelation 1:6, and the church is called 'the Israel of God' in Galatians 6:16. Twelve times twelve times a thousand is a number built from completeness, and chapter 14 describes the same people with the Lamb. On this reading the hearing and seeing are two views of one people, in a pattern like the Lion and the Lamb of chapter 5.

debates.bearing: The chapter does not demand one answer, and serious readers have held both for centuries. What is certain is that God's people are sealed before the harm, and that the multitude is not an afterthought but the same people at the same throne. The meaning for the reader is secure whichever view is taken.

debates.question: Are the 144,000 and the great multitude one group or two?

views.label: Two groups, Jewish believers and Gentile believers
views.case: The two scenes are introduced with separate formulas, 'I heard' and 'I saw', and one is numbered while the other cannot be counted. Some also point to the sealing taking place on earth, while the multitude is in heaven, and to the way Israel is distinguished in Romans 11 from the Gentiles.

views.label: One people, seen in two ways
views.case: In Revelation the hearing and then seeing is a habit of presentation, as with the Lion and the Lamb in 5:5 and 5:6. The number twelve thousand times twelve is a way of saying that no one is lost, while 'too large to count' says how many there are, and both end at the throne. Chapter 14 shows the 144,000 with the Lamb on Zion, and no one else is called out beside them there.

debates.bearing: Both readings take the multitude's salvation as God's gift in the Lamb's blood. If they are two groups, the chapter assures each; if they are one people, it assures them in two voices. In either case the promise to the church is the same, that no one who belongs to the Lamb is lost.

study.originalLanguages:
The word 'seal' is sphragis, a signet or the impression it makes, and the verb sphragizo, 'to seal', is used in verses 3, 4 and 5 to 8. John does not describe what the mark looks like, but the point of a seal is ownership and protection. The cargo that is sealed cannot be tampered with, and a seal on the forehead says openly to whom the person belongs. The verb is in the perfect passive participle in verse 4, 'those who have been sealed', the state of being sealed that has already been done.

The people sealed are the douloi, 'servants' or slaves, of our God, verse 3. The word is the one Paul uses of himself in Romans 1:1, and it chooses the language of belonging. They are marked as the slaves of a good Master and are therefore under his protection.

The multitude is described as 'too large to count', and the Greek says literally 'which no one was able to count', using the verb arithmeo, from which 'arithmetic' comes. The contrast with the 144,000, whose arithmos was heard, is built into the vocabulary. The four terms for the nations, 'nation, tribe, people and tongue', appear in several lists across the book, in varying order and with some varying words, which is the way John says 'all of humanity' without ever using the same formula twice. Palm branches in verse 9 are phoinikes, the palm, and the plural speaks of the multitude waving victory branches.

The elder says that the white-robed ones are 'the ones coming out of the great tribulation', hoi erchomenoi ek tes thlipseos tes megales. The participle is present tense, and the phrase has the article twice, 'the tribulation, the great one'. The present participle suggests a continuing stream and not a single event, and the double article speaks of a specific and well known affliction, which is what makes the phrase a point of debate about timing. The word thlipsis means pressure, the squeezing of an olive or a grape, and is the ordinary New Testament word for affliction, as when John calls himself a partner in the tribulation, Revelation 1:9.

The washing is told in the aorist: 'they washed their robes and made them white', eplynan and eleukanan, past actions with a sure result. The paradox is that blood makes things white. The elder gives the reason with 'for this reason', dia touto, the washing is why they are before the throne.

Their service is latreuo, the word used for priestly worship, performed 'in His temple', and the promise that God 'will spread His tabernacle over them' uses the verb skenoo, from skene, a tent. It is the verb of John 1:14, 'made His dwelling among us', and it recalls the Shekinah, the glory that rested on the tabernacle. The promise ends with poimaino, 'shepherd', future tense: the Lamb 'will be their shepherd', and 'will guide them' to springs of living water.

typology.type: The mark on the foreheads, Ezekiel 9:4
typology.fulfillment: In Ezekiel's vision a man with a writing kit marks the foreheads of those who grieve over the sin of the city, so that the executioners following him would pass them by. The correspondence is exact in form: a mark first, judgment after, and the marked are spared. The escalation is that the mark in Revelation is the name of God and of the Lamb, written on the forehead, Revelation 14:1 and Revelation 22:4, and that the New Testament says the seal is the Holy Spirit, Ephesians 1:13. The type falls short in its scope, since Ezekiel's mark protected people from a single city's fall, and the seal in Revelation protects for eternity.

typology.type: The Passover blood on the doorposts, Exodus 12:13
typology.fulfillment: The blood on the doorposts was a sign by which the destroyer passed over the house, and the people inside were safe because of the blood and not their own merit. John's multitude has made its robes white 'in the blood of the Lamb'. The correspondence is protection through blood, and the Lamb was in fact Passover's own symbol. Paul says 'Christ our Passover lamb has been sacrificed', 1 Corinthians 5:7. The escalation is that the blood now cleanses the person and not only marks the door. The type falls short in that the Passover protected one night, while the Lamb's blood secures a place before the throne forever.

At the feast Israel gathered palm and leafy branches and rejoiced before the LORD for seven days, living in booths as a memory of the wilderness. The multitude in white holds palms, and the LORD 'will spread His tabernacle over them', verse 15. The correspondence is the harvest joy and the dwelling of God with a pilgrim people. Zechariah 14:16 foresees the nations going up to keep the feast, which fits this crowd from every nation. The escalation is that God no longer shelters His people in booths but dwells with them, John 1:14 and Revelation 21:3. The type falls short because the booths were temporary and the feast had to be kept every year.

typology.type: The people numbered by tribe, Numbers 1
typology.fulfillment: Israel in the wilderness was counted tribe by tribe, and the tribes camped around the tabernacle in order. John's list is a numbering of the same kind, made complete and equal. The correspondence is that God knows and keeps His people by name and order. The escalation is that the throng around the throne is drawn from every nation, so that the nations are counted into Israel's tabernacle, as Revelation 21:12 and 21:14 show with the twelve tribes on the gates and the twelve apostles on the foundations. The type falls short in that the first numbering was of fighting men, and this one is of the redeemed.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first by the center of the throne. The Lamb is placed 'in the center of the throne', verse 17, so that He is both the one who is worshiped and the one who serves. The multitude cries 'Salvation to our God, who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb', verse 10, and the angels respond with a doxology addressed to 'our God'. John places the Lamb inside the worship that belongs to God alone, which is how the New Testament says that Jesus is divine, and a reader who has met chapter 5 will not be surprised.

It leads to Christ by blood. The multitude has washed its robes in the blood of the Lamb, a puzzling image in which blood makes things white. The paradox is the heart of the gospel, that the shed blood of the innocent Lamb is the only thing that cleans the stained. The prophet Isaiah had said that sins like scarlet could become white as snow, Isaiah 1:18, and 1 John 1:7 says that the blood of Jesus His Son cleanses us from all sin. The multitude brings no merit but a washing, and the verbs of verse 14 make the washing the reason for the standing.

It leads to Christ as the Shepherd. 'The Lamb in the center of the throne will be their shepherd', verse 17, is a strange sentence, a lamb that shepherds. Yet Jesus had called Himself the good shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep, John 10:11, and Ezekiel 34 promised that God Himself would shepherd His scattered flock and that He would set over them one shepherd, His servant David, Ezekiel 34:23. The Lamb is the one who was slain and also the one who leads. A reader who knows Psalm 23 will hear it fulfilled: green pastures and still waters become springs of living water, and the valley of the shadow becomes the great tribulation passed through.

It leads to Christ as the dweller among His people. God 'will spread His tabernacle over them', and the verb is the one John used of the Word who became flesh and 'made His dwelling among us', John 1:14. The tent over the multitude is Jesus in His glory, the same one who pitched His tent in Galilee. The promise of the end is the continuation of the incarnation.

Finally, it leads to Christ as the answer to the question of chapter 6. The sealed are not safe because they are strong, but because they belong to the Lamb. Paul says that there is now no condemnation for those in Christ Jesus, Romans 8:1, and the multitude in white is the picture of that sentence. A caution is in order: the chapter does not teach that Christians are excused from suffering, since the multitude has come out of tribulation. It teaches that they are brought through it, and that the Lamb is waiting at the other side.
study.god:
The chapter shows God as the one who protects before He judges. The four angels have power to harm, and the winds are held until the sealing is done. God is not slow to judge because He is soft, but because His first concern is for His servants, and He orders the timing of history around their security. That is a different sort of power from the show of force the empire displayed. The God of Revelation holds the winds like a shepherd holding a gate.

He is the God who knows His own by name and by number. The sealing of the tribes in equal portions, twelve thousand apiece, shows that nobody is lost in a crowd. Jesus said the Father knows the number of the hairs of our head, Matthew 10:30, and He calls His sheep by name, John 10:3. At the same time He is the God whose people exceed all counting, which is the promise made to Abraham long before, Genesis 15:5. The two pictures, precisely counted and beyond counting, belong to a God who is both exact and abundant, a God to whom nothing is too small to notice or too large to fit.

He is the God who receives worship, and the worship in this chapter is directed to Him in a particular order: salvation is ascribed to Him, and the angels respond with a sevenfold doxology that begins and ends with 'Amen'. The doxology lists blessing, glory, wisdom, thanks, honor, power and strength. It puts thanks into the list of the divine attributes, which is a reminder that gratitude is the right response to a God whose whole character is given freely. Salvation is described as His, the verb for it is not one the multitude has done but one they ascribe to Him. They cry 'Salvation to our God', admitting that it comes from Him and not from themselves.

He is the God who dwells. The promise of verse 15 says that He will spread His tabernacle over them. The one who sits on a throne is also the one who shelters. The transcendent and the near are joined, as in Isaiah 57:15, where the high and lofty One lives also with the contrite. Throne and tent are not rivals in this chapter.

And He is the God who comforts in detail. He does not simply promise 'no more suffering', but names the hunger, the thirst, the sun, the heat, and the tears, and promises to deal with each. The final act in the chapter is that God Himself wipes the tears away, a gesture of tenderness that belongs to a parent. For worship this means that we can sing at the throne and weep in our trouble in the same breath, because the God we praise is the one who will stoop to wipe our faces.

crossReferences.note: A man marks the foreheads of those who sigh over the abominations in Jerusalem, and those marked are spared when judgment comes. The sealing of the servants of God before the winds are loosed is built on this pattern, with the mark placed first and the harm held back until it is done.

The blood on the doorposts becomes a sign, and the destroyer passes over the houses where it is found. The protection of the sealed and the white robes washed in the Lamb's blood both go back to this Passover, where safety comes through blood and not through merit.

Paul says believers were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit when they heard and believed the gospel. This explains what the seal on the forehead means for the church today: it is the mark of belonging given to every believer, as the sign that they are God's own until redemption.

God promises that all the families of the earth will be blessed through Abraham. The multitude from every nation, tribe, people and tongue is the visible fulfilment of this, and shows that the nations are not shut out of Israel's story but gathered into it.

The new song says the Lamb purchased people for God from every tribe, tongue, people and nation by His blood. Chapter 7 shows the purchase complete: the crowd the song promised is now standing, and it is the same fourfold list from the same book.

At the Feast of Tabernacles Israel gathered palm branches and rejoiced before the LORD for seven days. The palms in the hands of the multitude gather the harvest joy of the festival into the heavenly scene, and the tabernacle promise of verse 15 completes the picture.

The prophet promises that God's people will not hunger or thirst, nor will scorching heat or sun beat down on them, because the One who has compassion will lead them to springs of water. Revelation 7:16 and 17 take this promise nearly word for word and apply it to the saints.

The Lord GOD will swallow up death forever and wipe away tears from every face. The final line of the chapter picks up this promise, which Revelation 21:4 repeats in full, so the elder's closing words are the prophet's hope arriving.

Daniel foresees a time of distress such as the world has never seen, and says that everyone whose name is in the book will be delivered. The 'great tribulation' of verse 14 draws on this, and the promise of deliverance for the written is the same one the sealed enjoy.

Jesus calls Himself the good shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep. Verse 17's lamb who shepherds is this same figure seen from heaven, and it explains why the one on the throne can be a lamb: the shepherd's way of caring was to die.

The 144,000 appear again, standing with the Lamb on Mount Zion with His name and His Father's name on their foreheads. The sealing of chapter 7 is shown to be a name written on the face, which reappears as the final reward of every servant in Revelation 22:4.

study.oneStory:
The story began with a people made to bear God's image and to live in His presence, and with a command to fill the earth. The fall emptied the garden of that presence, and the first promise was that a seed would come. Genesis 12 narrows the story to one family with the astonishing purpose that all the families of the earth would be blessed through them, and from then on the Bible is the story of that blessing being carried out. This chapter shows the harvest.

The number in verses 4 to 8 shows the story from Israel's side. The tribes had been a people of twelve, carried off, scattered, divided between north and south, and sometimes seemingly lost. Here they are numbered again, complete, with no one missing. It is God's answer to the exile, and to the long sense that the people of promise had been undone. The Lord who regathers is the Lord who has kept every name.

The multitude in verses 9 to 14 shows the story from the nations' side. The nations of Genesis 10 had been scattered at Babel into many languages, Genesis 11:9, and there the story of humanity splits. In Revelation 7 the languages are still there, nation and tribe and people and tongue, but they are standing in one place and speaking one cry. The division of Babel is not undone by erasing the differences but by gathering them before the throne. Pentecost was the sign of this, Acts 2:5 to 11, and this crowd is the finished work.

The ending of the chapter takes up the loss of Eden. Hunger, thirst, the heat of the sun and tears are all the effects of the curse on the ground, Genesis 3:17 to 19, and they are removed one by one. The shelter spread over the crowd is the presence that Adam and Eve lost when they hid among the trees. The tree of life and the river will appear in chapter 22, and the springs of living water in verse 17 are the first look at it.

The chapter sets up the rest of the book as well. The reader is told in chapter 7 that no one in the Lamb's flock is lost, and the following chapters of trumpets and bowls will be read against it. When the story ends in the new creation, the dwelling of God with man, Revelation 21:3, the 'tabernacle' that was promised in verse 15 is a whole city, and the people sealed and counted in this chapter live in it.

sermon.title: The Message and the Multitude
sermon.why: Begg preaches directly on Revelation 7:9-17, the vision of the great multitude in white robes before the throne, drawing out how this scene of countless worshipers from every nation should stir believers toward the mission of proclaiming Christ to every tribe and tongue, engaging the heart of this section's climactic scene.

quiz.q: Why do the four angels hold back the four winds at the start of chapter 7?

options.text: So that the servants of God can first be sealed on their foreheads.
options.note: Verses 1-3 give this exact reason for delaying the winds of judgment.

options.text: Because God had decided to cancel all further judgment.
options.note: Judgment resumes with the seventh seal in chapter 8; the winds are only delayed, not canceled.

options.text: Because the angels had lost the authority to act.
options.note: The text says the angels were 'given power to harm,' showing their authority is intact but restrained by command.

options.text: To allow the martyrs from chapter 6 to be resurrected immediately.
options.note: The delay concerns the sealing of God's living servants, not the resurrection of the martyrs.

quiz.q: How is the 144,000 described in verses 4-8?

options.text: A specific number, 12,000 from each of the twelve tribes of Israel, who are sealed.
options.note: Verses 4-8 give this precise breakdown by tribe.

options.text: An uncountable multitude from every nation on earth.
options.note: That description belongs to the group seen in verse 9, distinct in its numbering from the 144,000.

options.text: A group of twelve individual apostles.
options.note: The number is 144,000 drawn from Israel's tribes, not twelve apostles.

options.text: A group whose number is never specified in the text.
options.note: The text gives the exact number, 144,000, and its tribal breakdown, in full detail.

quiz.q: What does the great multitude in verses 9-10 cry out before the throne?

options.text: 'Salvation to our God, who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb!'
options.note: Verse 10 records this exact cry of worship.

options.text: 'How long, O Lord, until You judge those who dwell on the earth?'
options.note: That cry belongs to the martyrs under the altar in chapter 6:10, not to the great multitude here, who are already crying out in triumphant worship.

options.text: A demand for their persecutors to be punished immediately.
options.note: Their cry is one of worship and praise for salvation, not a demand for vengeance.

options.text: Nothing; they stand in complete silence.
options.note: The text explicitly describes them crying out in a loud voice.

quiz.q: According to the elder in verse 14, how did the great multitude's robes become white?

options.text: They washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.
options.note: Verse 14 gives this exact explanation.

options.text: Through their own moral effort and good works alone.
options.note: The text specifically credits the Lamb's blood, not unaided human effort, for making the robes white.

options.text: By surviving to the end of the great tribulation on their own strength.
options.note: They do come out of the great tribulation, but their robes are made white specifically by the Lamb's blood, not by their own survival or strength.

options.text: The text does not explain how their robes became white.
options.note: Verse 14 explicitly explains this: washed in the blood of the Lamb.

quiz.q: What is promised to the great multitude in verses 15-17?

options.text: God's tabernacling presence, no more hunger, thirst, or scorching heat, and the Lamb as their shepherd who wipes away every tear.
options.note: Verses 15-17 detail exactly these promises.

options.text: A return to earthly life to continue their former struggles.
options.note: The promises describe permanent heavenly rest and care, not a return to earthly struggle.

options.text: Only the removal of physical thirst, with no mention of God's presence or comfort.
options.note: The promise includes far more than physical relief; it includes God's tabernacling presence and the wiping away of every tear.

options.text: Continued exposure to persecution and tribulation without relief.
options.note: The passage promises the opposite: an end to hunger, thirst, scorching heat, and every tear.

questions: God held back judgment until His servants were sealed. Where do you need to trust that God's timing protects His people even when the world around you feels dangerous or uncertain?
The great multitude is 'too large to count, from every nation and tribe and people and tongue.' How does this shape the way you view believers who look, sound, or worship differently than you do?
Their robes were made white by the Lamb's blood, not by their own effort. Where are you tempted to rely on your own performance rather than resting in what Christ has already done for you?
The multitude came 'out of the great tribulation' into triumphant worship. What hardship are you currently in that you can trust God to bring you through, rather than around?

The Lamb Himself will be their shepherd, wiping away every tear. What tears are you carrying right now that you can bring honestly to Him, trusting that this promise is not only for the future but for today?

translationNotes.note: This tribal list differs from every other list in Scripture: Dan is omitted entirely and Levi, normally without a land inheritance, is included, while 'Joseph' replaces the more common 'Ephraim'; the variation suggests the number functions symbolically, picturing the complete people of God, rather than as a strict genealogical record.

The promise that they will never hunger or thirst, nor be struck by scorching heat, draws directly on Isaiah 49:10's promise to the exiles returning from captivity, now fulfilled fully for the redeemed before God's throne.

The image of the Lamb as shepherd leading to springs of living water echoes Psalm 23:1 and Isaiah 49:10, while God wiping away every tear directly quotes Isaiah 25:8's promise of the end of sorrow and death.
